I will freely confess to not understanding the module system properly. I kind of know what it does but here are some big things I don't know about its current status in the ecosystem.

1) What is the current status of Mathlib and the module system? I just found a file which starts

module

public import Mathlib.Algebra.Star.SelfAdjoint
public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dimension.StrongRankCondition
public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.FreeModule.Finite.Basic

import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.Torsion.Prod

My conclusion is that Mathlib now seems to have two different kinds of imports (public and not). However most files are just all pubilc imports. What is going on here? Are we in the middle of some kind of transition process? Or did it finish already?

2) In FLT we are still pre-module, because when the system was introduced there seemed to be some talk of automation which would modulize your repo automatically. Did this ever happen? Can I now move to the module system by running a script which puts module at the top of every file and public in front of every import? Is there an officially-sanctioned script which does this?

3) When FLT is modulized, how am I supposed to decide which imports are public and which ones are not? I have seen https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Source-Files-and-Modules/#module-scopes but it's one thing knowing the theory, it's quite another (at least as far as I can see) knowing what to do in practice. Is this also something which is going to be done automatically (I just run a script and it spends two days compiling FLT many many times with various choices of public removal until it finds a local minimum)?

Yes, moving to the module system made very liberal made use of @[expose] public section. I think the script you're looking for is Modulize.lean in the lean4 repo. It does essentially this, with an option to use meta sections as needed. Past that, experimentation with non-public imports seems pretty early, others can probably answer about this better than me.
How do I run this script on all the files in a repo? Or is that not the intended usage?

This is way too much simplified and probably wrong, but I think a first rule-of-thumb:

use public import for the files containing your defs and use a bare import for the files containing the API/lemmas about said defs.

and mathlib is barely at the start of the transition, having all public import plus the @[exposed] public section is basically equivalent to the situation before modules, which is what most mathlib files currently have.

Here's a slightly more principled approach; put the following in your lakefile:

def withGetModulizeLeanFromUrl (x : System.FilePath → LogIO Unit) : LogIO Unit := do
  let modulizeLeanSrc ← Lake.getUrl "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leanprover/lean4/refs/heads/master/script/Modulize.lean"
  IO.FS.withTempFile fun handle path => do
    handle.putStr modulizeLeanSrc
    handle.flush
    x path

module_facet modulize (mod) : Module := do
  Job.async do
    withGetModulizeLeanFromUrl fun modulizeLeanPath =>
      proc {
        cmd := "lean"
        args := #["--run", modulizeLeanPath.toString, mod.leanFile.toString]
      }
    return mod

library_facet modulize (lib) : Array Module := do
  (← lib.modules.fetch).mapM fun mods => do
    /- note: this may include modules from other libraries in the package if there are dependencies
    among them, but modulizing those is necessary to modulize these -/
    withGetModulizeLeanFromUrl fun modulizeLeanPath =>
      proc {
        cmd := "lean"
        args := #["--run", modulizeLeanPath.toString] ++ mods.map (·.leanFile.toString)
      }
    return mods

package_facet modulize (pkg) : Array Module := do
  let mods := Job.collectArray <|← pkg.leanLibs.mapM (·.modules.fetch)
  mods.mapM fun mods => do
    -- deduplicate, as dependencies between libraries will cause modules to appear in both
    let modSet : ModuleSet :=
      mods.foldl (init := {}) fun acc mods => mods.foldl (init := acc) .insert
    let mods := modSet.toArray
    withGetModulizeLeanFromUrl fun modulizeLeanPath =>
      proc {
        cmd := "lean"
        args := #["--run", modulizeLeanPath.toString] ++ mods.map (·.leanFile.toString)
      }
    return mods

Then you can run e.g. lake build MyLib:modulize, lake build @myPkg:modulize, and lake build MyLib.MyModule:modulize.

There are a few convenient things like this that I feel we could be doing with lake that I feel ought to be a part of some little lake_utils package, which Mathlib and such could depend on and get all the benefits of. (You then wouldn't need to change your own lakefile.)

I don't understand why the expose attribute interferes with the difference between rfl and by rfl:

module

public section

def foo : Nat := 23

theorem foo_def : foo = 23 :=
  -- rfl -- fails
  by rfl -- works

@[expose]
def bar : Nat := 23

theorem bar_def : bar = 23 :=
  rfl --works

I believe if the proof is exactly rfl, then Lean marks the lemma specially. This affects tactics like dsimp which only work with proofs that are exactly rfl. In other words, the "rfl-only" status is somehow part of the public interface of a theorem. As far as I can tell, this checks for the exact string "rfl". So, (rfl) is treated the same as by rfl.

This is mostly speculation because I don't know how dsimp works behind the scenes. But I think the reason for this is that if A.lean defines

public def foo : Nat := 23

@[simp]
public theorem my_theorem : foo = 23 := rfl

and B.lean contains example : foo = 23 := by dsimp, then the dsimp proof will just be rfl, which is actually not valid in the context of B.lean because foo is not exposed. So, this will be rejected by the kernel or some similar system. Thus, any public theorem that could potentially be used by dsimp must also just be rfl outside of the current file.

That being said, this is certainly surprising behavior and I wonder if there is a nicer solution to this problem. One potential solution would be to have a different way to indicate the "rfl-only" status of a theorem because that is part of the public interface.

I was thinking of requiring users to explicitly specify that their theorem is defeq, e.g. by requiring them to provide the @[defeq] attribute explicitly, but this seems like it would cause a lot of boilerplate and missed opportunities to take advantage of dsimp.

A more immediate fix would be to improve the error message. The note

Note: This theorem is exported from the current module. This requires that all definitions that need to be unfolded to prove this theorem must be exposed.

In my opinion, the message should explain that this limitation only applies to the literal text rfl and it should also mention @[defeq] and provide advice that using something like (rfl) bypasses this.

I propose that (rfl) be the canonical way to write a non-@[defeq] lemma whose proof is rfl. The reason for this is that (rfl) looks weirder than by rfl and is more likely to draw attention, which I think is a good thing because this pattern is not well known. "Ugly" patterns like (rfl) are justified when something unusual is happening, in accordance with the principle that good notation should be designed to make natural concepts easy to express and unnatural concepts hard to express.

Additionally, by rfl might be written accidentally, whereas if you see (rfl) it is clear that the author intended to bypass the rfl detection. Also sometimes by has different elaboration behavior than term mode, so someone attempting to replace by rfl with rfl might assume it is a bug in by that is causing only the former to get accepted, whereas someone trying to replace (rfl) with rfl and getting an error will immediately understand that some type of exact string detection is going on. Using (rfl) makes explicit the author's intention to bypass the rfl-detection and ensures the author is doing it on purpose, and by rfl does not do these things.

If the decision is made that the current @[defeq] behavior is fine, then over time (rfl) will become an idiom that people will learn about once they see it, whereas if we chose by rfl to be a canonical form, then most people will never learn about this until it bites them. Of course, another solution would just be to change the behavior of the automatic @[defeq] tagging.

We talked about this at the Portugal retreat. I think generally, there was agreement that the fact that syntax has such an important role here is a footgun. So in the future, the intention to mark the lemma as defeq should be made explicit, and should not be communicated by the proof being rfl vs rfl-in-disguise.
